planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, sandy, lean soil in full sun; sweet pea gladiolus follows the Cape winter-rainfall cycle, growing through autumn and winter and flowering in late winter through spring before going summer dormant. It takes its common name from the sweetly fragrant, pea-blossom scent of the flowers, not from any relation to true sweet peas.

directions: Plant corms in gritty, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun in fall; sweet pea gladiolus is a winter-growing Cape species native to sandstone flats and slopes of the Western Cape, producing large, showy flowers in shades of pink to mauve, speckled on the lower tepals, carried on wiry spikes from winter into spring. The flowers carry a notably sweet fragrance reminiscent of clove pinks, unusual among the mostly unscented hybrid garden gladiolus. Like other Cape winter-rainfall bulbs, it needs a bone-dry summer dormancy and sharp drainage to avoid corm rot, making a raised bed, gravel garden, or container culture the most reliable approach outside its native climate. This species has also naturalized in parts of Western Australia under compatible Mediterranean conditions.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in sandy, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun; this dwarf Cape species grows only 3-10 inches tall and follows a winter-growing, summer-dormant cycle, flowering in early spring with a light, pleasant fragrance. It is well suited to shallow pans and troughs where its small scale can be appreciated up close.

directions: Plant corms in sandy, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun in fall; kalkoentjie is a diminutive winter-rainfall species from the sandy flats and plateaus of the southwestern Cape, producing hooded, orange flowers boldly marked with yellow on the lower tepals, on stems rarely taller than 10 inches. A rare white-flowered form also exists in the wild near Villiersdorp. Because of its small stature and demand for lean, gritty soil, it performs best in shallow containers, alpine troughs, or raised sand beds where competing vegetation and excess winter wet can be kept away from the corms, going fully dormant and dry through summer. It multiplies steadily by offsets under favorable conditions, forming small colonies over a few seasons.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; evening-scented gladiolus grows through the Cape winter and blooms from late summer into early winter depending on elevation, opening dull brown to greenish-cream by day and turning bluish-mauve at dusk with a strong clove fragrance. This day-to-night color shift is a genuine botanical curiosity worth siting near a path or window.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall; evening-scented gladiolus is grown chiefly for its remarkable flowers, which appear dull earth-brown, tan, dull pinkish-red, or greenish-cream by day but transform each evening to a bright bluish-mauve, releasing an intensely sweet, clove-like fragrance that attracts night-flying hawk moths and owlet moths as pollinators. Native to clay slopes across a wide swath of the Western and Eastern Cape from the Cederberg to Port Elizabeth, it is more tolerant of clay-based soils than many of its sandier Cape relatives, though good drainage and a dry summer rest remain essential. Position it where the evening fragrance and color change can be enjoyed at close range, such as along a path or near an outdoor seating area used in the evening.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

common_name: The Bride Gladiolus (Hardy Dwarf White Gladiolus)

planting.note: Plant corms 4-5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun in fall for bloom the following late spring to early summer; this dwarf hybrid of Gladiolus cardinalis and Gladiolus tristis is markedly hardier than modern hybrid gladiolus, overwintering in the ground in zones 7-10. In zone 6 and colder, mulch heavily over winter or lift corms after bloom and replant in spring.

directions: Plant corms in well-drained soil in full sun in fall; 'The Bride' is a historic dwarf gladiolus dating to 1871, a pure-white sport of the Gladiolus x colvillei group (itself a cross of the Cape species G. cardinalis and G. tristis), producing slender spikes of small, funnel-shaped, snow-white flowers with a faint green to creamy mark on the lower petals. Unlike the tall summer hybrid gladiolus that dominate the trade, this compact, graceful type needs no staking, naturalizes well in mild climates, and blooms in late spring rather than summer. Feed with a potassium-rich fertilizer as spikes emerge and continue for a few weeks after flowering to build strong corms for the following year. Excellent for the front of a sunny border, in pots, or as an early, elegant cut flower.
